query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases and why catastrophic failure may occur? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, predicted observations relative to the starting-state baseline, applicable exposure boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Under elevated-temperature exposure, degradation and catastrophic failure in the additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA are governed by interfacial oxidation between the FCC matrix and its strengthening precipitates. This oxidation increases local misfit strain and promotes creep‐induced microcracking at these interfaces, with degradation accelerated in oxidizing environments.
generation.material_initial_state: Additively manufactured high-entropy alloy with composition Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 possessing an FCC matrix with ordered strengthening precipitates.
generation.intervention: Systematically vary the oxygen partial pressure during high-temperature (around 982 °C) exposure by switching between oxidizing and reducing (or inert) gas environments.
generation.conditions: Exposure at elevated temperatures (~982 °C) under controlled atmospheres with oxygen partial pressures ranging from high (oxidizing) to very low (reducing/inert).
generation.structural_mediator: The formation and spallation of thin oxide layers at the matrix-precipitate interfaces, which alter local misfit strain fields.
generation.mechanism: In an oxidizing environment, oxygen diffuses preferentially at the interfaces between the FCC matrix and the precipitates. This leads to the formation of oxides that, due to differences in thermal expansion and volume, induce stress concentration and accelerate localized creep deformation. The resultant microcracking at these weakened interfaces can propagate, culminating in catastrophic failure. In reducing environments, limited oxide formation minimizes these effects, preserving microstructural integrity for longer periods.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to a baseline inert environment, specimens exposed to oxidizing conditions will show increased oxide scale formation at matrix-precipitate interfaces, earlier onset of interfacial microcracking, accelerated creep rates, and a shorter time to catastrophic failure. Conversely, specimens in a reducing environment should exhibit reduced interfacial oxidation, slower creep kinetics, and delayed failure.
generation.baseline: Performance of the HEA under inert or very low oxygen conditions, where minimal oxidation occurs and the microstructure remains stable with lower creep rates and no accelerated interfacial cracking.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies at high temperatures (close to 982 °C) with gas compositions at the extremes of oxygen partial pressures (highly oxidizing vs. strongly reducing/inert).
generation.uncertainty: The exact threshold oxygen partial pressure needed to initiate significant interfacial oxidation and the quantitative relationship between oxide thickness, misfit strain, and the acceleration of creep remain to be determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of identical HEA specimens and expose them at 982 °C under rigorously controlled atmospheres: one set with high oxygen (oxidizing), a second set with very low oxygen (reducing/inert), and a control group in an inert atmosphere. Regularly monitor the microstructural evolution, focusing on the matrix-precipitate interfaces using SEM/TEM, and perform high-temperature tensile and creep tests to record mechanical performance over time.
measurements: Creep rate and time-to-failure under each condition
Extent and morphology of oxide layer formation at interfaces (via microscopy)
Onset and propagation of interfacial microcracks
Comparison of tensile yield strength and elongation at failure over exposure time
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no significant difference in interfacial oxidation, microcrack formation, or accelerated creep and failure is observed between oxidizing and reducing/inert conditions compared to the baseline, then the proposed mechanistic role of interfacial oxidation cannot be supported.

cited_evidence.text:
The High Temperature Tensile and Creep Behaviors of High Entropy Superalloy

Abstract: AbstractThis article presents the high temperature tensile and creep behaviors of a novel high entropy alloy (HEA). The microstructure of this HEA resembles that of advanced superalloys with a high entropy FCC matrix and L12 ordered precipitates, so it is also named as “high entropy superalloy (HESA)”. The tensile yield strengths of HESA surpass those of the reported HEAs from room temperature to elevated temperatures; furthermore, its creep resistance at 982 °C can be compared to those of some Ni-based superalloys. Analysis on experimental results indicate that HESA could be strengthened by the low stacking-fault energy of the matrix, high anti-phase boundary energy of the strengthening precipitate, and thermally stable microstructure. Positive misfit between FCC matrix and precipitate has yielded parallel raft microstructure during creep at 982 °C, and the creep curves of HESA were dominated by tertiary creep behavior.
